title: Verify the news
hook: if a wrongdoer brings news, verify it, lest you harm people unknowingly (49:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Abu Bakr, whose raised voice stands behind a verse on how to speak. Your line: the humble voice.

A screenshot arrives in the family group chat: something outrageous someone supposedly said. Within ten minutes it's been forwarded to three other groups, two aunts are furious, and nobody has asked the obvious question: is it real? The forward button is new. The problem isn't. In Medina, the commentators say, one unchecked account nearly sent armed men against a whole tribe. The verse tied to that story is a short rule about news.

Verse six, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." Evil-liver is Pickthall's word for fasiq, someone known to cross the line, whose word can't simply be trusted. Tidings is naba': news that carries weight, news people act on. And the command is one Arabic word: fatabayyanu. Make it clear. Find out. Here is the story commentators most often link to the verse. The Prophet ﷺ sent a man named al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to collect the zakat from the tribe of Banu al-Mustaliq. He turned back before reaching them and reported that they had refused to pay and meant to kill him. Anger rose in Medina, and in the version in Musnad Ahmad a party set out toward the tribe. On the way it met the tribe's chief, al-Harith ibn Dirar, coming the other way, puzzled that no collector had arrived. They had gathered the zakat and were waiting. The report was false. Commentators differ on the details, and some question parts of the account, but the shape is what the verse addresses. Notice the reason given: not just that lying is wrong, but that you'll harm people in ignorance and then be sorry. The responsibility sits with the listener, not only the speaker. In one of the recognized readings of the Qur'an, the same word is recited fatathabbatu: make sure, stand firm before acting. Two readings, one instruction: slow down before you strike.
screen: `FATABAYYANU: MAKE IT CLEAR.` · `NABA': NEWS PEOPLE ACT ON.` · `A FALSE REPORT ABOUT A WHOLE TRIBE.` · `THE LISTENER IS RESPONSIBLE TOO.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last week: was there something you passed on, out loud or with a forward, that you never checked? Don't scold yourself; just notice it, and hold one question ready for next time: who said this, and how do they know? If you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue.
Fatabayyanu: make it clear before you act, lest you harm people in ignorance, from 49:6. Today's word.
Your line: verify first. News is only as sound as its source. Day five hundred eighty-four, done.

howItsDone: Islamic scholarship built whole sciences on checking reports, above all the study of hadith chains and narrators; Muslim teachers today cite 49:6 when urging people to check news before sharing it.

original.note: Arabic: then make it clear, verify (49:6); also read fatathabbatu.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't spread lies.
what it means: when news would make you act against people, check it first, or you may harm them in ignorance.
what a scholar hears: the canonical readings of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recite fatathabbatu; the story of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah is the commonly cited occasion.
recall: a pledge sealed hand in hand

chat.says: Someone forwarded shocking news about a neighbor. What does Al-Hujurat say to do?
options: Verify it first, so you don't harm people in ignorance and regret it.
Share it quickly, since warning others matters more than checking it.
Ignore it, because the verse says every report from anyone is false.
